source.title: Optimal Nonlinearities Improve Generalization Performance of Random Features

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps random-feature dimension and measures generalization error against model complexity, testing double descent in a different model setting from deep networks.
record.gate_note: The text reports results on generalization error versus model complexity, including an explicitly described double-descent curve and its mitigation. Other double-descent results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps random-feature width k/m and reports generalization-error curves. For ReLU and Softplus it reports a double-descent peak at the interpolation point k/m=1, and it reports that task-optimized nonlinearities, which the authors equate with tuning the regularization scale, remove or mitigate the peak. This bears on V4 (the curve in a non-deep model class) and on V6 (the peak's dependence on regularization).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Optimized nonlinearities beat ReLU/Softplus on generalization and mitigate double descent, with a monotonic error decrease on synthetic classification. The authors also claim these nonlinearities remove the need to tune lambda. The abstract's mention of sample-size non-monotonicity is not tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps the feature dimension of random-feature models, whose first-layer weights are frozen, and optimizes activation mapping parameters; it does not reproduce a deep-network size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed curve depends on the activation function; the paper reports steep double descent for ReLU and Softplus but monotonic decrease for the proposed optimal nonlinearities. It also compares different regularization settings, though it does not report an optimally tuned regularization sweep.
record.peer_reviewed: Asian Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 222, 2023
record.problems: The double-descent curves are presented in figures without numerical error values or stated uncertainty intervals. The real-image results rely on normalizing-flow preprocessing, and the Tiny ImageNet appendix notes fluctuations associated with the small number of samples.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible double-descent results were left out. Other plotted training-error and accuracy results were excluded because the claim versions concern test/generalization error.

untested.parts: No size sweep of deep networks; the model is a random-feature model with a frozen first layer.
No sample-size sweep, although the abstract mentions non-monotonicity in sample size.
Only random-feature models are tested; no other model classes, and no claim about subsuming the U-shaped curve.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
Label noise is not varied (Delta=0 in the classification runs). Multiple peaks are not examined. Lambda is not explicitly tuned to its optimum; only two fixed lambdas are compared.

missing.what: Comparison of ReLU/Softplus generalization curves at lambda=10^-1 (Fig. 3(a)) vs lambda=10^-4 (Fig. 3(b)). Authors say this confirms that regularization mitigates the peak.
ReLU/Softplus generalization-error curves on CIFAR10 and Tiny ImageNet. These are needed to tell whether a baseline peak exists on real data.
Inverted ('upside-down') double descent in test accuracy, especially for ReLU on CIFAR10.

record.verdict_notes: The model is a random-feature model, a class close to the random Fourier features used in Belkin et al., so for V4 this is a near-replication in a shallow model class rather than a new class. All double-descent evidence is figure-only, with no numbers or error bars. The 'optimal' nonlinearities are chosen per feature matrix by grid search on generalization error (validation error for real data), so their monotone curves partly reflect per-k tuning.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random features with a frozen first layer, not a sweep over the size of deep networks as stated in this version.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No sweep over training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
Tests random feature models only; it does not establish the curve across other model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, or samples.

The study does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak. It compares some fixed regularization settings but does not tune regularization to test this version.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

statements.problem: Synthetic peak removal and real-image mitigation are reported, but 'only mitigate' overstates the evidence for a remaining real-image peak.
